What mak's me so vnnimbly ryse, That did descend so fleete? There is no vp-hill in the skyes; Clouds stay not feathered feete. Some Lady heere, is sure too blame That from Loves starry skyes, Hath shot some Beame, or sent some flame, Like Lghtning, from her Eyes. I'le rowle me in Auroras Dew, Or lye in Tethis bed; Or from coole Iris begge a few, Pure Opale shewrs new shed.
Thy wings are sing'd: and thou canst fly But slowly now, swift MERCVRY. Taxe not the Starrs, with what the Sunne, Too neere aproch't (insens't) hath done. Nor Dew, nor shewers, nor sea can slake Thy quenchlesse heate, but Lethes lake.
Though I have earn'd it with the sweat of my browes in Ianuary, yet I am glad I saw it, for there never was such a sight seene. The Triumph. The Triumph of ALBANACTVS. They did so, for some rid me. Some trode on my toes. Some cryed, some kept it in; for my part, I confest all, for feare I should have beene p • est to death. Were not yours so too? Where stood you? You had the better friends sir, I pray where sate you? Is not your studdy backward? with a shop-light in it, where one can see nothing but the skye? Why then you saw no Triumph. If what I saw was but a shew, what you saw was but a shadow, or at the most a Vision. For it seemes your body kept home, though your spirit walkt. To confute that Heresie of yours, I have gone, and seene, and know, but I will say nothing. Faith sir, I am very full indeede. ALBANACTVS CAESAR from his sumptuous Pallace, through the high-streets of ALBI POLIS rid Triumphing, on a Chariot, made— Sir I saw him not as he was borne, naked, but since you affect such brevity, I saw the King and a great deale more, and so I turn'd my backe, and went away. When you beginne to tell your dreames, I'le not iogge you, till you wake of your selfe. I am not angry, but a little short-winded vpon oc casion. Yet to give you some satisfaction because you have done me wrong. Before CAESAR March't Captive Kings, with their hands bound. And Ladies, with their Armes acrosse, furious wild Beasts, great Giants, and little Dwarfes with Lictors, and Pictors, and a number of Prie • ts that were as you would have them, In their shirts. These with certaine Princes that were behind him: made vp a Triumph too great to come out of any mortall mans mouth. I meane in words. But as you hunt me you would hunt a Hare off her leggs. I graunt it, But yet graunt me one Request deare Platonicus? Goe but with me to the Amphitheater. Yes. I should sleepe at such a sight. All together, and so (I hope) are you Lifting vp the stone I stumbled at. To see what lyes vnder it. If there lye not a Morall vnder it, then have you taught me false Doctrine.
What sight Publius? Whose Tryumph? Didst thou see it? No, I thinke, some rid. Though thy body was pincht, thine eyes were feasted. Yes. I stood not, In my studdy. I confesse it, what of that? But I did, and a true one, thine was but a shew. It did so. And travelled to better purpose then most men doe, that goe, and see, and say, but know nothing. That's impossible; The meate thou hast lately fed vpon, is so windy, out it must, thou wilt burst else. Purge then, and tell thy Doctor all. Of wood, perhaps guilt, perhaps gold. But I will save you all those charges, if you will goe on to the Per sons, and let the Pagents alone. Nay good Publius, now thou art too briefe. Nay prethee be not angry. That's most certaine. I confesse thou hast made more haste, then good speede: But for a supplement to thy lame Story, Know, I have seene this brave ALBANACIVS CAESAR, seene him with the eyes of vnderstanding, vew'd all his Actions; look't into his Mind: which I finde armed with so many morall vertues that he dayly Conquers a world of Vices, which are wild Beasts indeede. For example Ambition, is a Lyon; Cruelty, a Beare; Avarice, a Wolfe. Yet He subdues them all. To be short, no Vyce is so small, to scape him: Nor so great, but he overcomes it: And in that fashion he Triumphes overall the Kings, and Queenes that went before him. All his Passions, are his true Subiects: And Knowledge, Iudgment, Merit, Bounty and the like, are fit Comma ders, for such a Generall, Th • se Triumph with him, And these are the Princes you saw about him. And this Publius, is more then you can finde in the streete. What's that? To Gaze. Why beforehand I know there will be Gladiators, Saltators, and sights to please the People. Wert not thou better stay here, and see CAESAR present himselfe to this fayre Goddesse, seeking sweete rest, after all his labors. Then after a Play, thou art all for a Pryze. At this time, I am. For I will goe with thee, if it be but to teach thee to Reade in thy owne Booke. Outsides, have Insides, Shells, have Kernells in them. And vnder every Fable, nay (almost) vnder every thing, lyes a Morrall. What art thou doing Publius. To what ende? What should lye vnder a stone, but a Worme, or a Hoglouse. Such thankes have they that teach such Sch • l lers. Come away Foole, they beginne to throng to the Theater.
speeches.Pub: See it, yes, and feele it too. Every one there (I can assure you) went not vpon his owne feete.
Sit not secure, nor thinke in ease Still vndispleas'd, your selues to please: Diana, Chast Diana stoope, And helpe to wound this war like troope. Love is grown wise, and meanes to bring To his smart Bowe, a double string. Behold our Marke? taks't thou not pride In such a Glory to devide?
Wants Love a Bowe, or shaft of mine? This suit will make my Crescent shine. I doe, I doe, since I am sure, When we two ioyne, our flames are pure.
As pure, and Cleere, as ALBAS skin, As her faire Fame, or thoughts within: Pure as my selfe; nay pure like Thee, Now Love is that which Love should be.
speeches.Peace: Frighted by Day; And in the Night diseas'd, I fled to Heaven, and left the World displeas'd. F • nd Men that strive more for a Province there, Then looking vpward to possesse a Sphere. Yet vanquish't and Victorious, both at last, Their weary Limmes, on my soft Bed would cast.
speeches.Two 2: Lyons, and Lambs togeather lye, When Lovly Peace stands smiling by Temples and Townes by thy stay'd hand, First learne to Rise, And then to Stand.
speeches.All 5: 'Tis not the Laurel Tree that brings, Anointing Oyle for sacred Kings: Those Princes see the happiest Dayes, Whose Olive Branches stand for Bayes.

Earths Rulers, stay! Yes: and will streight employ yee All.

N • ptune to Sea, And let no Sayle, Meete ALBIONS Fleete, But make it veile. Bellona Arme, That Foes may see, Their Lillies kept by Lyons be. Their fruitfull fields (Cebele) make Pay Centupl • for all they take. And let Both Indies (Pluto) meete, And lay their wealth at ALBAS feete.
speeches.The foure God;: When Peace commands such pleasing things, From Love and Time wee'l steale their wings.
